newsitem.title: FRANCE: S. Korea strike goes on until law quashed - union.
newsitem.headline: S. Korea strike goes on until law quashed - union.

text.p: South Korea's outlawed umbrella union group said on Tuesday strikes would continue unless President Kim Young-sam quashed laws which would allow firms to dismiss workers and tighten the noose on unions.

The warning came despite a stunning U-turn by President Kim, who said the law, forced through parliament in a dawn session on December 26, had backfired on the economy because of strikes and would be sent back to parliament.

"We are calling on the government to make a categorical statement of intention to annul the law and open talks," Yoon Young-mo, spokesman for the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions (KCTU), told a news conference in Paris.

"The reason the trade union movement is calling for a firm commitment is that we are used to being misled," he said. "The statement from the government is not clear. These two laws need to be declared null and void."
"The plan of the KCTU is to continue for the moment the one day a week strike, which is on Wednesday this week," Yoon said, echoing comments in Seoul by his federation's president, Kwon Young-kil.
Yoon in Paris to attend an OECD review of South Korean labour law, stuck to condemning the government stance when questioned about Kim's U-turn.

"Korea, like other countries in the world is faced with the challenge of (trade) globalisation. The government wants to take the road by itself and doesn't want social and union organisations to take part," he said.
"We believe these (laws) are an attempt by the Korean government to return to...authoritarian rule, from a government unable to adapt to the changes in Korea towards a more pluralistic society."
He said his views were shared by members of other South Korean trade unions who are in Paris for the meeting at the Organisation for Economic Co-Operation and Development.

The OECD, an organisation espousing free-market economics, has found itself in a highly uncomfortable position since the outbreak of labour unrest in South Korea, having just admitted Seoul to the international group in December.

OECD Secretary General Donald Johnston said earlier this month he was deeply concerned by the situation in South Korea because of his organisation's attachment to human rights, including labour rights.
Johnston also noted at the time that South Korea had pledged to review its industrial relations after the issue was raised by several OECD members during membership talks.

"What are the OECD going to do about this now," said Rodney Bickerstaff, a British Trade Union Congress member who attended the news conference. "This is the OECD blessing something it wouldn't have done had this (the laws and strikes) happened before Korea was let in (to the OECD), he said.
President Kim said labour strife had defeated the law's aim of revitalising the economy, according to a spokesman. Production losses have been estimated at more than $3 billion.

Kim also agreed to reopen debate on a controversial law reviving a once notorious domestic spy agency and told heads of three main political parties he would instruct officials to suspend arrest warrants served on strike leaders.
